lines.speaker: Aeacus
lines.text: Protesilaus — what are you doing? Let go of Helen.
lines.note: Flat procedural opener. Aeacus is not shocked, just managing a disturbance.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: She's why I'm dead, Aeacus. I left my house half-built. I left my wife a widow on our wedding week.
lines.note: Genuine grievance, not self-pity. The specificity is what makes it land.

lines.speaker: Aeacus
lines.text: Then blame Menelaus. He's the one who dragged you all to Troy over a woman like this.
lines.note: 'A woman like this' — not cruel, just the gatekeeper's weary accounting.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.note: He releases Helen and pivots. Quick, almost comedic redirect.

lines.speaker: Menelaus
lines.text: Not me, my friend — Paris is your man. He was my guest, and he walked off with my wife. Every law of gods and men, broken. He doesn't owe you a strangling — he owes one to every Greek and barbarian whose blood was spilled because of him.
lines.note: Menelaus is in full courtroom mode: rehearsed, righteous, and very much enjoying not being the one getting choked.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: Better still. [grabs Paris] You, then. Ill-starred Paris. I'm not letting go.
lines.note: Δύσπαρι — 'Ill-starred Paris' / 'Ill-Omened Paris' — a pun on his name used as an insult.

lines.speaker: Paris
lines.text: You're being unjust, Protesilaus — and to a fellow sufferer, at that. I'm a lover too. The same god had me in his grip. You know how it works: it's not voluntary, a spirit drives you where it wants, and there's nothing you can do about it.
lines.note: Paris is entirely charming and entirely unrepentant. The argument is real — Eros as compulsion was standard — but he delivers it with the ease of a man who has made it before.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: Fine. [pause] I wish I could get my hands on Eros while I'm at it.

lines.speaker: Aeacus
lines.text: I can answer for Eros too, if you want a fair ruling. He'll say he may have been responsible for Paris falling in love — he'll give you that much. But your death, Protesilaus? That one's on you. You forgot you had a new bride. The moment the ships touched the Trojan shore, you leapt out ahead of everyone else — recklessly, desperately — because you were in love with glory. And that's why you were the first man killed in the landing.
lines.note: Aeacus delivers this as a judicial summation, not a lecture. The irony — Protesilaus died for the same reason Paris sinned, an uncontrollable eros, just a different variety — is left for the audience to notice.

lines.speaker: Protesilaus
lines.text: Then I'll give you my counter-argument, Aeacus — and it's the better one. None of that was my doing. It was Fate. It was the thread that was spun for me from the beginning.
lines.note: He lands this with perfect sincerity. The irony is that it is exactly Paris's argument, one step removed.

lines.speaker: Aeacus
lines.text: Quite right. [pause] So why are you blaming these two?
lines.note: The punch line is delivered as a simple procedural question. Aeacus doesn't even look up.
